title: Non-union work and joining the union with Streeman
summary: Streeman's non-union band earned above scale with 25-26 nights a month and refused union offers until hotels went closed shop around 1939.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: And we joined the union, Dick, when the hotels went closed shop, which I think was around 1939. Uh huh. And Streeman used to get all the work in town, like I told you before. Uh huh. In the early years with Streeman, we were getting work 25, 26 nights a month.

And we were non-union and we were making more than union scale. And that was the reason we didn't join a union. We didn't have to join a union. The union was actually jealous of us that we were making that amount of money. And they offered us into the union three different times. And I used to think Al Streeman was kidding me.

But until he showed me the letter that the union wanted us in and offered the whole group in for nothing without any initiation fee or anything. Uh huh. And we didn't go. And, and in 39 when the unions went, uh, the hotels all went closed shop, which meant that you had to be union to play in any hotel. Uh huh. When we began losing work, you know, because we were playing for big oil companies and sororities and fraternities and what have you. Uh huh. And nearly all your work was in hotels. So I told Al, I said, Al, why don't you call a meeting at your house and talk it over with the fellas in the band? And I said, let's join a union. And talk about joining a union. I said, you're losing all your good work, all your two lane work. You played for all these, uh, Rush Week, you'd get all this work. And two lane fraternities besides regular, sororities, fraternities. And in the old days, they, they were more fraternity and sorority dances than they are nowadays. Man, every week, every two weeks, every month there were sorority dances. Now they give them once a year. It's nothing like the old days. There was plenty parties in the old days. Of course, the economy I guess has a lot to do with that. Everything is so high now. You know, that's the reason why, you know, I have a sorority dance every month now. I dance at the other, in the tea room every week like they used to have. There was a lot of work for musicians in the old days. And there's still a lot of work, but I mean it's a whole different situation nowadays. But the price is the way they are, you know.
